title: Limits of Schatten Best Approximants: Universal Convergence and Failure of Strict Spectral Selection

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Limits of Schatten Best Approximants:
Universal Convergence and Failure of Strict Spectral Selection
Ziyang Liu1

Yunxuan Wang2

Yao Shi3∗

1

National University of Singapore
2
ETH Zürich
3
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
For 1 < p < ∞, let Yp minimize the ℓp -norm of the residual singular values when a finite
complex matrix is approximated from a complex linear subspace. We prove that Yp always
has a limit as p → ∞, and that the limit is a spectral-norm best approximant. The proof uses
definability in the o-minimal real exponential field. We then show that this limit need not be the
strict spectral approximant, whose residual singular-value vector is lexicographically least. An
explicit two-dimensional subspace of 3-by-3 matrices gives a limit whose third residual singular
value is 272 /28, whereas the strict residual has third singular value zero. We also determine
the exponentially small scale and the first correction. The matrix-size threshold is sharp: strict
spectral selection holds when the smaller matrix dimension is at most two.

Theorem 1.1 (Universal convergence). For every A ∈ Cm×n and every complex linear subspace
M ⊆ Cm×n , the limit

The conclusion is unconditional: uniqueness of the spectral-norm best approximant is not
assumed. Compactness alone would give only convergent subsequences. The additional input is that
the unique minimizer Yp depends definably on p in the o-minimal real exponential field; bounded
definable curves cannot oscillate indefinitely. We give the complete argument in section 2.
It remains to identify the limit. For vectors ρ, τ ∈ Rn0 , we say that ρ is lexicographically smaller
than τ if, at the first index where they differ, the corresponding coordinate of ρ is smaller. The
strict spectral approximant Y st is the unique element of M for which σ(A − Y st ) is lexicographically
least among the vectors σ(A − Y ), Y ∈ M; see [8, p. 309] and the original construction in [6, 7]. In
particular, those references provide the existence and uniqueness asserted in this definition.

The curve p 7→ vp is commonly called the Pólya path. The strict Chebyshev approximant is the
element of V whose residual coordinates, rearranged in nonincreasing order of absolute value, are
lexicographically least. Descloux proved that vp converges to this strict approximant as p → ∞;
his finite-set hypothesis is exactly the finite-dimensional vector setting just described [1, Theorem,
pp. 1020–1022]. Linearity matters here: Egger and Huotari showed that after V is replaced by an
arbitrary closed convex set, the Pólya path may fail to converge or may converge to a point other
than the same lexicographically defined strict uniform approximant [2, pp. 212–216]. The question
below keeps the approximating set linear and instead replaces coordinate absolute values by singular
values.
Ziętak proposed the corresponding matrix statement in [8, Conjecture 1.1, p. 309]: in the
notation above, Yp → Y st . Grover and Gupta restated the conjecture and proved it in several special
cases, including the entire range n0 ≤ 2 [3, Equation (5) and Theorem 3.7]. Their general compactness argument identifies every convergent subsequence only as a spectral-norm best approximant;
uniqueness of that approximant then gives convergence [3, Remark 3.5(1)]. Compared with that
remark, theorem 1.1 removes the uniqueness hypothesis on the spectral-norm best approximant.

The two theorems separate existence from identification. The Schatten path always selects a
spectral-norm best approximant, but it does not in general select the lexicographically strict one.
Moreover, 3-by-3 is the smallest square size in which this failure can occur; more generally, the
threshold n0 = 3 is sharp. The example is real symmetric, but the theorem uses its complex span
and hence covers the usual complex formulation.
After proving universal convergence, the counterexample proof has three steps. First, we identify
the strict approximant directly. Second, symmetry and a two-dimensional comparison reduce the
finite-p problem to two positive real parameters. Finally, two exact first-order optimality equations
give the limit and both asymptotic formulas without a perturbative remainder estimate. The last
section explains the resulting nonlexicographic selection mechanism.

2

Universal convergence of the Schatten path

We prove theorem 1.1 by combining a uniform bound with one imported result from o-minimal
geometry. The following paragraph states the complete version used here. The real exponential field
Rexp is the ordered real field together with the function x 7→ exp x. A set is Rexp -definable if it can
be described, allowing fixed real parameters, by finitely many equations and inequalities involving
the field operations, order, and exponential, together with Boolean operations and quantifiers over
real variables. A map is definable when its graph is.
Wilkie’s theorem says that Rexp is o-minimal: every definable subset of the real line is a finite
union of points and intervals [5]. The monotonicity theorem then gives the precise consequence we
need: if f : (α, ∞) → R is definable, then for some α0 > α its restriction to (α0 , ∞) is continuous
and either constant or strictly monotone [4, Chapter 3, Theorem 1.2]. Consequently, every bounded
definable real-valued function on a half-line has a finite limit at infinity.

The strict approximant and the finite-exponent reduction

We first settle the lexicographic problem. This also records explicitly why the example lies outside
the case of a unique spectral-norm approximant.

5

Why the limit selector is not lexicographic

Theorem 1.1 rules out nonconvergence of the Schatten path itself. The remaining question is which
spectral-norm best approximant the path selects. In the example of theorem 1.2, the set of such
approximants contains more than one point, and the exact proof exposes why the selected point is
not the strict spectral approximant.

exact optimality equations instead. If w is held in a compact subinterval of (0, 27) and t is small,

We call L a virtual level: it is produced by optimizing the trade between the first two singular values
and is not a singular value of the strict residual. The segment
{(t, w) : t = 0, 0 ≤ w ≤ 27},
is the nonnegative part of the two-level face: throughout this segment, the first two residual singular
values remain fixed at 28 and 27. Moving along it increases the coefficient of the gain until the
physical third singular value w reaches L. The w-optimality equation makes the collision precise
and even gives the correction p(L − wp ) → L log 4.
This behavior is consistent with the known partial results. Grover and Gupta prove convergence
of the top residual singular-value block to its strict counterpart; if the largest strict-residual singular
value is simple, the next equal-value block converges as well [3, Proposition 3.4 and Theorem 3.6].
The strict residual here has singular values (28, 27, 0), so these conclusions read
σ1 (A − Yp ) → 28,

σ2 (A − Yp ) → 27.

The failure occurs at the third level, the first level not controlled by those results.
There is also no conflict with Ziętak’s pointwise characterization [7, Theorem 1]. The finitedimensional subspace M is closed and convex, so the theorem says that for every fixed Y ̸= Y st
there is a threshold p0 (Y ) such that
∥A − Y st ∥Sp < ∥A − Y ∥Sp

whenever p ≥ p0 (Y ).

The threshold may depend on Y . In the present example the minimizer itself moves with p, with the
transverse coordinate tp on the exponentially small scale (27/28)p ; pointwise eventual comparison is
therefore not uniform on the two-level face described above.
Finally, the mechanism differs from Descloux’s vector theorem for linear families. There each
residual coordinate is the absolute value of an affine function, so the top-level objective is polyhedral
once the residual signs are fixed; the smooth quadratic cost above has no analogue. Thus the
obstruction is spectral, not a failure of finite dimensionality or linearity. Nor does it contradict the
convex-set counterexamples of Egger and Huotari [2], where linearity is absent.
